# Big Short Team talk Market Turmoil, Tariffs, and Lessons from the Financial Crisis

First listed: 2025-04-07 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [YouTube: Big Short Team talk Market Turmoil, Tariffs, and Lessons from the Financial Crisis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VqQ8glQSFM) - 2025-04-07

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

The former Big Short team debates tariffs rather than presenting one shared forecast. Danny Moses expects a retreat; Eisman expects a month of retaliation with tariffs maintained before negotiations. The subsequent pause supports Moses and contradicts Eisman's timing. Eisman's no-China-negotiation claim also fails against May talks. The group emphasizes gross-exposure reduction, credit spreads, leverage and executable prices, drawing on 2008 experience. China exports routed through Vietnam do not justify adding them again to total exports, and US trade-worker retraining programs existed. Historical success stories remain unverified recollections; severe drawdowns are conditional scenarios, not unconditional Eisman targets.

Full discussion and post-crisis recollections reviewed, excluding the duplicated opening montage as a claim locator. Important disagreements and uncertain rapid interjections are retained. Primary evidence resolves tariff timing, adjustment-program existence, CVS revenue and the 2008 short-sale ban; it does not validate every retrospective claim or infer motives from subsequent price direction.

## Material claims

<a id="youtube-3VqQ8glQSFM-c001"></a>
### 001. The announced reciprocal tariffs use a trade-imbalance formula rather than actual equivalent foreign tariff rates.

**Right** | Danny Moses | explanation | major

[Source at 2:34-3:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VqQ8glQSFM&t=154s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

USTR describes a goods-deficit/import proxy with common assumptions, supporting the central criticism.

Qualification: The discussion alternates between correct imports language and imprecise references to what partners buy; no exact misstated denominator is silently repaired.

Assessment test: Distinguish arithmetic validity from economic justification.

- [Reciprocal tariff calculations](https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/files/Issue_Areas/Presidential%20Tariff%20Action/Reciprocal%20Tariff%20Calculations.pdf) (2025-04): The formula uses bilateral goods deficits and imports as a proxy, with common elasticity/pass-through assumptions. It does not separately total each country's VAT, tariffs and regulations.

**Unresolved** | Danny Moses | explanation | major

[Source at 3:05-3:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VqQ8glQSFM&t=185s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The timing mechanism is plausible, but the magnitude of pain and firm-level adjustments were not independently measured.

Assessment test: Track capacity lead times, prices, margins and supply-chain relocation.


<a id="youtube-3VqQ8glQSFM-c003"></a>
### 003. The administration will walk back these tariff rates because the initial package is too disruptive.

**Right** | Danny Moses | forecast | major

[Source at 3:24-4:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VqQ8glQSFM&t=204s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The April 9 order suspended most country-specific rates; May 12 reduced China's reciprocal component after talks. The retreat occurred, while the asserted motive is not fully proved.

Assessment test: Keep the observed policy reversal separate from causal explanations.

- [Reciprocal tariff modification](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/modifying-reciprocal-tariff-rates-to-reflect-trading-partner-retaliation-and-alignment/) (2025-04-09): Most country-specific reciprocal tariffs were suspended for 90 days with a 10% rate retained, while China's reciprocal rate increased to 125%.
- [China tariff negotiations and reduction](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/05/modifying-reciprocal-tariff-rates-to-reflect-discussions-with-the-peoples-republic-of-china/) (2025-05-12): After discussions with China, the reciprocal tariff component was reduced to 10% for 90 days effective May 14, reversing much of the escalation. Other tariff layers remained.

<a id="youtube-3VqQ8glQSFM-c016"></a>
### 016. Ten-year yields can reverse higher if the term premium rises despite weaker growth.

**Right** | Danny Moses | analytical principle | major

[Source at 10:24-10:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VqQ8glQSFM&t=624s) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

Long yields can rise if an increase in term premium exceeds a decline in expected short rates.

Conditional reasoning: In the decomposition long yield = average expected future short rates + term premium, a term-premium increase larger than the expected-rate decline raises the long yield. This identity does not predict that such an increase will occur.

Assessment test: Estimate expected-rate and term-premium components separately.

<a id="youtube-3VqQ8glQSFM-c041"></a>
### 041. NAFTA improved GDP but failed to create jobs and devastated industrial communities.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 26:42-27:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3VqQ8glQSFM&t=1602s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

CBO supports small GDP gains and small early aggregate employment effects; that does not settle later regional losses or justify attributing all industrial decline to NAFTA.

Assessment test: Separate aggregate, regional, technological and China-trade effects.

- [Effects of NAFTA on US-Mexican trade and GDP](https://www.cbo.gov/sites/default/files/108th-congress-2003-2004/reports/report_0.pdf) (2003-05): CBO finds small positive GDP effects and small employment effects through 2001, with most major trade-balance fluctuations attributable to other factors. This is not a full 1994-2025 employment estimate.

### 050. Credit spreads measure the extra yield on risky debt over a comparable risk-free benchmark.

Conditional reasoning: For comparable risky-debt yield y_R and benchmark Treasury yield y_T, the simple spread is s=y_R-y_T. Option and liquidity differences must be accounted for before interpreting all s as default risk.

Assessment test: Use matched duration, currency and option-adjusted measures.

Conditional reasoning: If Treasury yield falls 50 basis points and credit spread rises 100, all-in risky borrowing yield rises 50. Therefore Treasury direction alone cannot determine borrower financing costs.

Assessment test: Compare actual financing yields and issuance access.

## Framework and tools

- Preserve disagreement rather than aggregate a panel into one forecast.
- Distinguish tariff persistence conditions from subsequent changed policy.
- Separate gross exposure from net market direction.
- Examine credit spreads alongside Treasury yields.
- Model the equity residual under leverage.
- Do not assume regulators share private analysts' information.
- Check executable bid/ask prices rather than trust marks.
- Combine loan-pool data, fieldwork and management interviews.
- Require contemporaneous records before crediting retrospective success.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Trade-deficit tariff formula
- Export/GDP comparisons
- Nike earnings multiples and downside scenarios
- Treasury yields, term premium and refinancing needs
- Long-short gross exposure
- HYG and risky-debt spreads
- CVS revenue and leverage example
- Mortgage securitization performance databases
- OTC CDS marks and two-way quotes
- Housing site visits
- Moody's downgrade and delinquency data

## Source cautions

Opening introduces Steve Eisman, Danny Moses, Porter Collins and Vincent Daniels. Named prompts and long answer blocks support attribution; rapid interjections sometimes do not. Claims with uncertain voices are explicitly Uncertain speaker and excluded from automatic Eisman attribution. Daniels is also called Vinny. The final host and named historical recollections are distinguishable from guest conclusions.
- Recorded April 4 morning but published April 7; Monday forecasts concern April 7 and are not made after that session.
- No speaker markers; several fast overlapping contributions remain unattributed.
- The opening panic-attack montage is repeated later and is not used as substantive timing evidence.
- FrontPoint, SVB, SIV, Moody's, Ray McDaniel and Greg Lippmann have caption spelling errors.
- The 50% market drawdown is a guest possibility that Eisman rejects; his 25-30% is also conditional.
- The OptionOne5% loss threshold is explicitly uncertain in the recollection.
- China total export/GDP must not be confused with direct exports to the US.
